<!-- Generated by SiteFrames render from Tests/Api/round2-parity.json. -->
I use the same domain names for cmdlet parameters, C# configuration and fluent calls. PowerShell keeps numeric duration parameters with units and default-off switches; C# keeps TimeSpan values and Boolean properties.

The contract covers **108 commands**, **1140 parameters** and **314 reachable public types**. The metadata gate checks names, types, sets, positions, defaults, nullability and member paths. Rendering and triplet tests check behavior.

Table and List remain named shortcuts to Show-Console’s shared view implementation. Read-* returns answers; New-ConsoleForm/Menu defines a question workflow; Show-ConsoleApp runs a persistent reactive application.

Typed Options on export, form, menu and replay operations expose the corresponding C# configuration. I can pass a PowerShell hashtable, for example `Export-ConsoleFrame -Format Html -Options @{ Width = 100; Padding = 8 }`. Options and individual settings are mutually exclusive; the supplied request is not modified.

Callback properties use `.Configure(item => item.Action = …)`. C# invokes a delegate-valued property before considering an extension with that name; Configure assigns the callback without invoking it.

## Fluent construction and nesting

Ui is the fluent entry point: New-ConsolePanel becomes Ui.Panel(), named settings stay in the chain, and nested Content uses c.Panel(panel => …). Initializers retain constructors. Factories accept no positional configuration; the recorded primary inputs below are the only exceptions. Chart, Progress and kind-selected inputs materialize their existing typed options through the shared Build operation.

## Parameter-set mappings

A structural parameter set can select a different request model. The metadata gate checks these mappings separately and includes both update requests in its public-member coverage.

<tr><td><code>ConsoleMonster.Interactive.TreeSelect.Filter</code></td><td>CSharpOnly: Retained tree filtering belongs to the embedded control rather than the object exploration constructor.</td><td>Set Filter on the TreeSelect returned by New-ConsoleTreeSelect.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ConsoleMonster.Interactive.TreeSelectInputOptions.Explorer</code></td><td>CSharpOnly: The PowerShell constructor adapts InputObject through its member-access and traversal-budget policy.</td><td>Use New-ConsoleTreeSelect -InputObject; C# callers can provide an ObjectExplorer.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ConsoleMonster.Widgets.LayoutRegions.NarrowBelow</code></td><td>CSharpOnly: Responsive regions are composed through the typed layout container.</td><td>Construct LayoutRegions in PowerShell or C# and pass it to Show-ConsoleApp.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ConsoleMonster.Widgets.LayoutRegions.ActiveRegion</code></td><td>CSharpOnly: ActiveRegion is live layout state used when no region owns focus.</td><td>Call Activate(key) on the retained regions container.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ConsoleMonster.Widgets.LayoutRegions.Gap</code></td><td>CSharpOnly: The inter-region gap belongs to the typed responsive container.</td><td>Set Gap on LayoutRegions before passing it to Show-ConsoleApp.</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>

## .NET host integrations

The PowerShell formatting, help and progress examples run inside a compiled PSCmdlet on its owning pipeline thread. The generic-host and ILogger examples configure .NET lifetimes; their PowerShell tab launches the same project. These options remain explicit C# integration settings.
